title: Assessing misinformation recall and accuracy perceptions: Evidence from the COVID-19 pandemic
screen_reason: National survey of U.S. adults (n = 1,045, Lucid/Qualtrics, 2-3 May 2020) reporting the percentage of respondents who said they recalled seeing prominent COVID-19 misinformation headlines (37% origins/government response; 30% treatments), plus the authors' placebo-corrected 'true recall' estimates. These are shares of survey respondents reporting encounter with misinformation, i.e. RECALL. The belief/accuracy-perception findings (Findings 2-4) are susceptibility measures and are excluded.

estimates.platform: Not platform-specific (headline claims that had circulated widely on social media and in the media)
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who self-reported recalling seeing prominent misinformation headlines about the origins of / government response to COVID-19
estimates.value_raw: On average, 37% of respondents reported recalling prominent false claims about the virus's origins/the nature of the government's response
estimates.denominator: 1,045 U.S. adults surveyed through Qualtrics via the Lucid platform (quota sample matched to the U.S. population on age, gender, ethnicity and region)
estimates.definition: respondent answered 'yes' to 'Do you recall seeing this claim about COVID-19 reported or discussed in recent months?' for a prominent misinformation headline in the origins/government-response category; figure is the average across the headlines in that category
estimates.misinfo_def: "misinformation headlines that had circulated widely on social media", identified by searching "news coverage in major U.S. newspapers and prominent fact-checking websites"
estimates.source_quote:
On average, 37% of respondents reported recalling prominent false claims about the
virus’s origins/the nature of the government’s response, and 30% reported having seen prominent
misinformation headlines about COVID-19 treatments.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Respondent self-report of recall. The headline stimuli themselves were selected by the authors from searches of major U.S. newspaper coverage and prominent fact-checking websites; no inter-coder reliability reported. Each respondent saw 10 of a pool of 22 headlines, randomised.
estimates.moderator_quote:
we administered a national survey of U.S. adults through Qualtrics from
May 2–3, 2020 (n = 1,045). Respondents were recruited via the Lucid platform, which employs quota
sampling to produce samples matched to the U.S. population on age, gender, ethnicity, and geographic
region.
estimates.notes: Headline self-reported recall figure for the origins/government-response category, averaged across the headlines in that category. The exact per-headline values are only in Figure 1 and are not printed in the text.

estimates.platform: Not platform-specific (headline claims that had circulated widely on social media and in the media)
estimates.measure_type: placebo-corrected 'true recall': % recalling prominent misinformation about COVID-19 origins/government response minus % recalling invented placebo headlines in the same category
estimates.value_raw: true recall of prominent false claims about the virus's origins/government response was approximately 11%
estimates.denominator: 1,045 U.S. adults surveyed through Qualtrics via the Lucid platform (the difference is taken between two percentages of this same sample)
estimates.definition: percentage self-reporting recall of actual prominent misinformation headlines minus the percentage self-reporting recall of the invented 'placebo' headlines in the same topical category (the Allcott & Gentzkow 2017 metric)
estimates.misinfo_def: "misinformation headlines that had circulated widely on social media"; placebo headlines are "false claims of equal plausibility ... that we invented and that had not circulated widely on social media or other news outlets"
estimates.source_quote:
We estimate
that true recall of prominent false claims about the virus’s origins/government response was
approximately 11%. Perhaps more importantly, our estimate of true recall of misinformation about fake
treatments for COVID-19 was just over 3%.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Self-reported recall, corrected by subtracting self-reported recall of researcher-invented placebo headlines; 95% confidence intervals shown in Figure 1 but not printed numerically.
estimates.moderator_quote:
We estimate true recall as
the percentage self-reporting recall of actual prominent misinformation claims minus the percentage self-
reporting recall of the placebo headlines in the same category (Allcott & Gentzkow, 2017).
estimates.notes: JUDGEMENT CALL for an adjudicator: 'true recall' is a difference between two shares of the same sample, not a raw share of respondents, so it is not a plain prevalence estimate; it is however the paper's own headline figure, stated verbatim ('approximately 11%'), and is the placebo-corrected version of the 37% row above - hence definition_variant=true and borderline=true. If the review pools only raw self-reported shares, drop this row and the treatments equivalent.

estimates.platform: Not platform-specific (headline claims that had circulated widely on social media and in the media)
estimates.measure_type: placebo-corrected 'true recall': % recalling prominent misinformation about COVID-19 treatments minus % recalling invented placebo headlines in the same category
estimates.value_raw: our estimate of true recall of misinformation about fake treatments for COVID-19 was just over 3%
estimates.denominator: 1,045 U.S. adults surveyed through Qualtrics via the Lucid platform (the difference is taken between two percentages of this same sample)
estimates.definition: percentage self-reporting recall of actual prominent COVID-19 treatment misinformation headlines minus the percentage self-reporting recall of the invented 'placebo' treatment headlines
estimates.misinfo_def: "misinformation headlines that had circulated widely on social media"; placebo headlines are researcher-invented false claims that had not circulated widely
estimates.source_quote:
We estimate
that true recall of prominent false claims about the virus’s origins/government response was
approximately 11%. Perhaps more importantly, our estimate of true recall of misinformation about fake
treatments for COVID-19 was just over 3%.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Self-reported recall corrected by placebo-headline recall; 95% CIs in Figure 1 only.
estimates.moderator_quote:
Following the metric created by Allcott & Gentzkow (2017), we estimated true recall as the difference in
self-reported recall rates between prominent misinformation and placebo headlines.
estimates.notes: Value stated as 'just over 3%'; recorded as 3 with the verbatim wording in value_raw. Same judgement call as the origins/response true-recall row.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (a) 'true recall of pandemic misinformation averaged 7%' across all substantive categories - a pooled average of the two category-level true-recall figures already recorded, kept out to avoid double counting (verbatim in the Essay summary and Implications). (b) Recall of REAL headlines (58% origins/response, 50% treatments) - the numerator is accurate information, not misinformation. (c) All accuracy-perception figures (61% correctly identified treatment misinformation as false, 60% for placebos, 46% for origins/response, 61% for Chinese-source claims, 'one in five said they were true', 41% correctly identified real treatment headlines as true) - these are belief/discernment, explicitly excluded. (d) Regression marginal effects for Trump approval (14%, 10%, 11% more likely to believe) - belief, and effect sizes not prevalence. (e) The 78% Kaiser Family Foundation figure cited in the Implications section is a figure the paper cites from elsewhere (R8). (f) Placebo-headline recall percentages appear only in Figure 1 and are not printed in the text, so they could not be recorded.

rob.design: Cross-sectional online survey of 1,045 U.S. adults fielded through Qualtrics on 2-3 May 2020; respondents recruited via Lucid, a non-probability opt-in panel using quota sampling matched to the U.S. population on age, gender, ethnicity and geographic region (no response rate reportable). Each respondent evaluated 10 headlines randomly drawn from a pool of 22 (real, prominent misinformation, placebo) across two topics, plus 2 of 3 Chinese-source headlines. Misinformation stimuli identified by author searches of major U.S. newspapers and prominent fact-checking websites; no inter-coder reliability reported for stimulus selection. Recall measured with a single yes/no/unsure item per headline; a placebo-headline correction is applied to address false recall. Robustness checks excluding speeders reported in the appendix. Sample demographics benchmarked to census figures in Appendix Table A1.
